newsitem.title: USA: Pan Am sees "cash-positive" first year.
newsitem.headline: Pan Am sees "cash-positive" first year.

text.p: Pan Am World Airways Inc Chief Executive Officer Martin Shugrue said on Tuesday he expects the airline to be "cash positive" in its first year of operation and profitable thereafter.
Pan Am, which began trading today on the American Stock Exchange, returns to the skies on Thursday, five years after the original Pan Am collapsed.
The new Pan Am will be a much smaller operation than its predecessor, which dissolved in the aftermath of the bombing of Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland.
The original Pan Am, a pioneer in commercial aviation, is still being liquidated in federal bankruptcy court.
Bearing the original name and logo, the new Pan Am will operate a fleet of three wide-body Airbus Industrie A-300 aircraft, which have an average age of 13 years, Shugrue said.
Within a year, service will be expanded to include up to nine aircraft, he said.
Shugrue said the new Pan Am is better positioned than most upstart carriers, due to a strong brand name and solid financing.
The company has cash on hand of about $25 million, and revenues are expected to reach $78 million in the first year, he said.
Shugrue declined to forecast results beyond the first year but said he expects Pan Am to see "significant growth in revenues in year two over year one."
Pan Am's costs will run about $0.06 per available seat mile, below the industry average of about $0.085, Shugrue said.

With no debt, outsourced aircraft maintenance and entry-level wages, the airline will be able to keep costs below industry averages, he said. Pan Am will manage and inspect the work of its maintenance contractors.
Pan Am has alliance pacts with 12 small and mid-sized international partners such as Eygpt Air and Iceland Air, and is in talks with a dozen other carriers, he said.
International operations will comprise about a third of Pan Am's operations, he said.
Shugrue served as vice chairman and chief operating officer of the old Pan Am, and families of some of the victims of Flight 103 had opposed his involvement with the new Pan Am.
"Pan Am has a rich history that includes a lot of firsts and milestones in the industry," he said. "But in the midst of all that glory, there are some downsides.

"But just as we can't take credit for all that success, we can't take the blame for those problems. We're a new company with a proud name. And we're hoping to restore that brand name to the shining star it once was."

Starting Thursday, Pan Am will offer flights from New York's John F. Kennedy Airport to both Miami and Los Angeles. Service will be expanded to include San Francisco, Chicago and San Juan, Puerto Rico, within the first year.
Pan Am recently merged with Frost Hanna Mergers Group Inc, which formerly traded on the Nasdaq Bulletin Board.
